beats.text: This is me in a phone store with a pen in my hand about to sign for a free twelve hundred dollar phone.
Free. From a phone company. The same people who charge me a fee for having a fee.
Spoiler.
That free phone cost me about eleven hundred dollars more than buying one. By the end of this video you'll know the three questions that make the salesman put his pen down.
But most people click away before that part which is exactly what the phone company wants.
So it starts on a Saturday. My screen has a crack shaped like Florida and I walk into the store.
The store is bright and cold and smells like new plastic. Every wall is covered in phones that cost more than my first car.
A very friendly salesman named Chad already has a pen out. Great news! This phone is twelve hundred dollars but today it's zero.
Me hearing the word free in a phone store.
And this isn't some sketchy store. All three big phone companies ran this exact deal on the newest iPhone.
There are balloons. There's a sign that says today only. It has said today only since I was in high school.
So I do what most of us do. I sign without reading a single word. And I feel like a genius.
Me signing a three year contract without reading it.
Then Chad turns the card reader around. Great news. That'll be ninety dollars today.
Ninety dollars? For a free phone? Chad says it's sales tax. On the full price. Even when my price is zero.
To be fair you'd pay that tax anywhere. But that was my first hint that free means something different in that store.
Chad's face when I ask why a free phone has tax.
A month later I open my first bill to admire the word free. And there's a charge. Phone payment. Thirty three dollars.
Right under it there's a credit for the exact same amount. One cancels the other. So I pay nothing. Phew.
I show my bill to my mom and she says that's not free honey that's a payment wearing a mask.
But look at what that really means. I bought a phone on a three year loan. And every month they send me a coupon that covers the payment. Thirty six coupons.
It's like a restaurant that gives you a free steak but serves it one bite a month. And only if you're still sitting at the table.
Me three years later still sitting at the table for the last bite of steak.
So in plain words my free phone is a loan I never notice. As long as I never stand up.
And then I read the offer again. Slowly this time. The coupons only work on the most expensive plan in the store. Ninety dollars a month. For one line.
Be honest. Do you know what your own plan costs right now? Most people don't. And the phone companies love that.
It comes with extras. Like a giant hotspot. I don't know what a hotspot is. I've never hotspotted in my life.
Me paying for a giant hotspot I will never use.
My brain trying to understand my phone plan.
So let's play a game. Door A. The phone is free and the plan is ninety a month.
Door B. You pay the full twelve hundred for the exact same phone and put it on a plan that costs twenty five.
Three years later which door is cheaper and by how much? Put your number in the comments. I'll wait.
Everyone in the comments picking door A.
Hold that guess. Because that night I fell down a rabbit hole. Who came up with free phones?
In two thousand seven Steve Jobs walks on stage with the very first iPhone. Up to six hundred dollars.
A year later the next one shows up at one hundred ninety nine dollars. And the lines go around the block.
People camped outside stores in sleeping bags. For a phone. I wouldn't camp outside for my own wedding.
The phone didn't suddenly get cheap to build. The phone company paid the rest. And you paid them back inside your monthly bill for two years.
Everybody hated those contracts. So a phone company boss in a bright pink T-shirt stood on stage and killed them.
A few years later the others dropped contracts too. We were free! Well. Sort of free.
Because the companies still needed you to stay. So they invented something that feels nicer than a contract. The monthly coupon.
And then they stretched it to three years. So the contract never died. It just put on a party hat with the word free on it.
The two year contract coming back in a disguise.
So I grab a napkin. Because all serious math happens on napkins.
Door A is ninety a month. Door B is twenty five. So the free phone plan costs me sixty five dollars more every single month.
Sixty five dollars a month is a gym membership I won't use plus a nice dinner. Every month. Gone.
Over three years that's more than two thousand three hundred dollars extra. Now be generous and take away the phone I got for free.
What's left is about eleven hundred dollars. That's what free cost me. And that's the number your guess had to beat.
Me looking at the napkin.
So where does that money go? One big carrier sold its phones for billions less than they cost last year. It's right there in their own reports.
They can lose money on phones because the monthly bills bring in way more. Like tens of billions more.
It's a pet shop that gives away the goldfish for free and then sells you the water every month for three years.
Phone companies selling me water.
And it works. In a typical month fewer than one customer in a hundred walks away.
So I decide I'll be that one customer. I'll take my free phone to a cheap plan. How hard could it be?
First I check if a twenty five dollar plan is even real. It is. And this part is a little insulting.
One of the best known cheap plans runs on the same towers as the expensive one. Because the big company owns it.
Same story across the street. Remember the cheap phone company from those Ryan Reynolds ads? A big carrier bought it for more than a billion dollars.
So the cheap brand and the expensive brand are cousins. They have the same grandpa. And grandpa gets paid either way.
So it's the same water in a fancier bowl. The cheap one can slow down when it's busy. But it's the same towers.
Expensive plan versus cheap plan.
So I call to cancel. And the nice person says great news. You can leave any time you like.
You'll just owe us the rest of the phone today. All twelve hundred dollars. Because the moment you leave the coupons stop but the loan doesn't.
And my phone is locked. It only works with the company that sold it until every last dollar is paid.
It's like buying a car that only drives on one company's roads. Until it's paid off.
That lock is a real fight in Washington. Regulators proposed making companies unlock phones after sixty days. Then this January one big carrier got permission to keep its phones locked longer.
The companies say locks stop thieves. Consumer groups say locks stop you from shopping around. That's a political fight. Now you know the rule.
For me the rule meant one thing. The only way out of free cost twelve hundred dollars.
And three years is long for a phone. You'll drop it. Or you'll want the new one. And then Chad calls with great news about fresh coupons.
The deal even took my old phone. It needed a trade in. So my Florida phone was going in a mailbox even though it worked fine.
My old phone worked fine. It had a crack shaped like Florida. That's not broken. That's character.
To be fair if you'd pay for that big plan for three years anyway this deal is a real discount.
The trick only works on people like me. People who'd pay less but can't put twelve hundred dollars on the counter. Honestly that's most of us.
That's the real product. It isn't the phone. It's a customer who can't afford to leave.
Phone companies looking at customers who can't leave.
But I had one thing left. The receipt. And at the very bottom was a line Chad didn't circle.
Quick note. This is education and not advice. Your own contract is the boss.
The line said returns. Big carriers give you a short window to bring the phone back. Usually two weeks. One gives you a month.
There's a restocking fee of around fifty dollars. I check the calendar. It's day thirteen. And I'd been too lazy to mail my old phone.
Me realizing being lazy saved me.
So now I have choices. And so do you. One. Keep the phone you already own and move it to a cheaper plan.
Two. Buy your next phone unlocked from the maker. So no phone company holds the leash.
Three. Take the free phone with your eyes open. Because you did the napkin math and it really is cheaper for you.
And whatever you pick ask three questions in the store. What's the plan price? How many months? And what do I owe if I leave?
Watch the pen go down when you ask the third one.
So on day thirteen I walk back into the store. Chad is already reaching for the pen.
Chad goes great news Dave! We've got a watch that's also free!
And I go great news Chad. I'm returning the phone.
Chad stopped smiling for the first time all year.
It cost me a restocking fee of fifty five dollars. The cheapest lesson I've ever bought.
I kept the Florida phone. Crack and all. And moved my number to the twenty five dollar plan. Zero signatures.
And the cheap plan? Same towers. Same calls. Same memes. I can't tell the difference and I've been looking very hard.
So every month sixty five dollars stays in my pocket. I drop it in a jar. In about a year and a half that jar buys the phone outright. Unlocked. No coupons. No Chad.
And yes I kept the pen. It was the only thing in that store that was actually free.
So before the pen comes out add up the plan and the phone over all three years.
Next time my friends take me out to celebrate and somebody says the five most expensive words in friendship. Let's just split it evenly.
Subscribe. It's free. Actually free. No coupons. And you can leave any time.
